summary: p-limit is a single-purpose library: one function that runs promise-returning functions with a concurrency limit. Sixteen files, no source directory, no build step. index.js holds the whole implementation, index.d.ts holds the types, and test.js, index.test-d.ts and benchmark.js check behaviour, types and speed respectively.

districts.name: The Whole Town
districts.purpose: The library is the repository root: implementation, types, tests, benchmark, readme and recipes sit side by side.

districts.name: The Measuring Yard
districts.purpose: A single benchmark harness used by benchmark.js to compare concurrency strategies.

districts.name: Civic Offices
districts.purpose: One workflow that runs the tests, plus the security policy.

importantModules.role: The entire implementation: a yocto-queue of pending calls, an active counter, and a resumeNext step that starts the next call as one finishes.
The public contract: pLimit, limitFunction, the LimitFunction type with activeCount, pendingCount, concurrency, map and clearQueue.
The behaviour suite: concurrency limits, argument passing, queue clearing and error propagation.
Type-level tests, so the .d.ts is checked rather than merely shipped.
Timed comparison of the limiter under load, run against the harness in scripts.
The full documentation: install, usage, the API for every exported member and the caveats.
Worked patterns for common cases, kept out of the readme so the API reference stays short.
Declares the package as ESM with one runtime dependency, yocto-queue.

strengths: One file does one thing: the concurrency limiter is small enough to read in a sitting, and there is no build step between source and published package.
Types are tested, not just declared: index.test-d.ts checks index.d.ts the way test.js checks index.js.
The library carries exactly one runtime dependency, so the install footprint of using it is nearly nothing.
Documentation is split between a reference readme and a recipes file, which keeps the API listing readable.
Zero open issues, with CI on every push through a single workflow.
concerns: Everything lives at the repository root, so the project has no structure to grow into if it ever gains a second module.
The queue behaviour is subtle (a promise is enqueued to preserve execution context) and that reasoning lives only in comments inside index.js.
